subject: Application - Senior Site Reliability Engineer (Remote, EU/CET)
paragraphs: I am applying for the Senior Site Reliability Engineer role on the Platform team. The description asks for someone who works across boundaries, taking reliability, security and the developer experience of shipping as one problem, and that is the shape of the work I have done for four years: a fleet declared entirely in code, where a change is not finished until a gate has read the built artifact back and the machines carrying it are still healthy.

Concretely, one flake declares thirteen NixOS hosts: pinned inputs, an SSH certificate authority instead of shared keys, SOPS-encrypted secrets, and a task interface as the only operator surface. A sentinel records job status, generation age, disk and pressure-stall figures to a ledger every fifteen minutes and pages when a state is not ok, pressure stall being the kernel signal that a machine is thrashing before anything visibly breaks. The services on it are Go and Python, and the mail archive is PostgreSQL with versioned migrations, rehearsed restores and disk-pressure alerting. On-call is one person, so the alerting had to be honest rather than generous.

The security half is not a separate project for me. Vulnerability work is a scheduled pipeline over the CISA KEV catalogue, matched against what the fleet actually runs, so patching is driven by what is exploited rather than by what is loudest. Least privilege shows up as short-lived certificates, per-host keys and no shared user credentials; network policy as nftables rules with a default deny. I have not been through a SOC 2 or ISO 27001 audit, so audit readiness would be new work rather than something I can claim, but the habits those frameworks ask for, inventory, change records, least privilege and evidence that a restore really works, are already how the fleet is run.

What I do not bring is the stack itself: no production AWS, no Kubernetes or Terraform (Nix is my infrastructure language), no Datadog, and no Neo4j or Snowflake. I have built the smaller equivalent of each, I learn tooling quickly, and I would rather say it now than have it surface in a system-design interview. On location: I am in south-west Germany, CET, inside the remote window you describe. Germany is not on your preference list, so I would rather ask than assume. There is no relocation on my side, the timezone overlap is full, and I can travel for retreats and the occasional on-site. I also work with coding agents daily rather than talking about them: this fleet's change loop, checks and coordination log are agent-operated, which is my closest honest answer to the AI-assisted workflow your description names.
